pass.title: A satellite's Doppler shift records its motion
pass.mini: A navigation receiver counts the carrier cycles of every satellite; the count's rate is the Doppler shift. Each satellite rises approaching and sets receding, at up to several hundred metres per second.
pass.text: Every navigation receiver counts the carrier cycles of the satellites it hears, and the rate of the count is the Doppler shift: the speed at which the satellite comes closer or moves away, 19 cm per cycle on GPS L1. On 10 April 2025 the receiver at Wettzell, in Bavaria, heard each satellite rise while closing in, pass its nearest point and set while moving away, at up to several hundred metres per second [1]. The curves are the fitted solution of this site: orbits, receiver positions, the Earth's GM and rotation, all adjusted to the Doppler alone. The Earth and the orbit on the left are to scale with each other.
pass.verdict: Would favour the flat model: speeds that a receiver held on a plane fits as well as a free one.
ball.title: From a flat map to a ball, by the Doppler alone
ball.mini: {{nStaAll}} receivers start on a flat map. Fitted to one day of satellite Doppler, every orbit unknown, they settle on a ball around the point the satellites orbit, {{rMin}} to {{rMax}} km from it.
ball.text: One day of carrier-phase Doppler from {{nStaAll}} receivers of the International GNSS Service on {{nSat}} GPS, Galileo and GLONASS satellites [1]. The fit starts with the receivers laid on a flat map (left, orange) and the Earth's GM 25 % too small; the satellites move under Newton's gravity, a flattening term and the pull of the Sun and the Moon [2]. Iteration after iteration each receiver moves to where the measured speeds put it. At the end they sit on a ball around the centre of the orbits: on the right, every receiver's distance from that centre falls into the band {{rMin}}–{{rMax}} km. The wire sphere is drawn at 6,371 km for reference only. GM and the rotation come out within a fraction of a part per million of the accepted values [3]. Held on a plane instead, with everything else free, the best fit misses the speeds by {{flatRms}} m/s, where the ball leaves {{rms}} mm/s.
ball.verdict: Would favour the flat model: receivers held on a plane fitting the Doppler as well as free ones, or a fit started on a plane that stays on it.
radius.title: Every receiver at the same distance from the centre of the orbits
radius.mini: Fitted to satellite Doppler alone, {{nStaKept}} receivers on every continent end {{rMin}} to {{rMax}} km from the point the satellites orbit: a ball, flattened at the poles (1/{{ellInvF}}).
radius.text: Each dot is a receiver of the International GNSS Service, placed by one day of satellite Doppler and nothing else [1]: its distance from the centre the 77 orbits go round, against its latitude. All lie between {{rMin}} and {{rMax}} km, nearest at the poles and farthest at the equator. An ellipse through them gives an equatorial radius of {{ellA}} km and a flattening of 1/{{ellInvF}}, close to the 6,378.1 km and 1/298 of the reference ellipsoid [2]; what is left, {{ellRms}} km, is mostly the receivers' heights. The best plane through the same receivers misses them by {{planeRms}} km.
radius.verdict: Would favour the flat model: receivers whose distances from the centre of the orbits spread over thousands of kilometres, as on a plane, rather than gathering into a narrow band.
kepler.title: Kepler's third law at three heights
kepler.mini: Three constellations to scale, each satellite at the period its own GM gives; each orbit predicts the measured Doppler to a few mm/s. GLONASS, GPS and Galileo, from {{aR}} to {{aE}} km, agree on GM to {{kepSys}} ppm.
kepler.text: Kepler's third law says that for everything orbiting one body, the period squared over the orbit's size cubed is the same: n²a³ = GM. The animation draws the three navigation constellations to scale, each satellite turning at the period its own GM gives. Each orbit was fitted to one day of Doppler from {{nStaAll}} receivers [1], and checked the way every orbit is: from the orbit, the satellite's speed toward each receiver is predicted, then compared with what the receiver measured. For GPS satellite G32 over Wettzell the two differ by a few millimetres per second, out of several hundred metres per second. With each satellite free to have its own GM, the {{nKep}} satellites give the same value to {{kepSpread}} parts per million, and the medians of GLONASS ({{aR}} km), GPS ({{aG}} km) and Galileo ({{aE}} km) agree to {{kepSys}} ppm. The forces of the Earth's flattening and of the Sun and Moon are kept in the motion [2].
kepler.verdict: Would favour the flat model: satellites at different heights needing different GM for their periods, so that no single attracting mass explains their orbits.
kepgm.title: One GM at three heights, satellite by satellite
kepgm.mini: Each of {{nKep}} satellites gives its own GM from its own orbit. From GLONASS at {{aR}} km to Galileo at {{aE}} km they agree to {{kepSpread}} ppm, with no slope.
kepgm.text: Each point is one satellite: the GM its own orbit asks for, fitted to one day of Doppler from {{nStaAll}} receivers [1], in parts per million around the common value, against the size of its orbit. GLONASS ({{aR}} km), GPS ({{aG}} km) and Galileo ({{aE}} km) sit at three heights and give the same GM: the {{nKep}} satellites agree to {{kepSpread}} ppm, the three medians to {{kepSys}} ppm. A failure of Kepler's third law would tilt the three groups or pull them apart. The two isolated Galileo points are the two satellites on eccentric orbits. The Earth's flattening and the Sun and Moon are kept in the motion [2].
kepgm.verdict: Would favour the flat model: GM values that drift with the height of the orbit, so that no single attracting mass explains the three constellations.
flat.title: The flat model, given every freedom but one
flat.mini: Same satellites, same data, everything free except that the receivers must lie on one plane: the best fit misses the measured speeds by {{flatRms}} m/s, {{flatRatio}} times worse than receivers left free.
flat.text: One satellite's speed seen from Wettzell through the day (dots), from one day of Doppler at {{nStaAll}} receivers [1]. Blue: the solution with the receivers free, which leaves {{rms}} mm/s. Orange: the best solution with every receiver held on one plane, its tilt, its height and the positions on it free, the satellites on Newtonian orbits around a centre anywhere, GM, the rotation, the clocks and the air as free as for the globe. It leaves {{flatRms}} m/s: half its misfits exceed {{flatQ50}} m/s. Two different starts were tried and the better kept.
flat.verdict: Would favour the flat model: a plane of receivers that fits the Doppler to a few millimetres per second, as the free solution does.
